title: The Humanoid Robotics Funding Race: What the Money Tells Us About Commercial Readiness
author: Lars Talbert, Founder
description: Nearly $11.7 billion in disclosed capital has gone into humanoid robotics. Not one of the best-funded companies in the category has a humanoid you can buy. The companies that do are the ones that raised the least.

sections.title: The Empty Quadrant
sections.content: Plot capital raised against deployment stage for every humanoid company with a disclosed funding figure, and one region of the chart comes up empty. There is no company that has both raised serious money and put a humanoid into general commercial availability. The data comes from The Robotic Life’s Humanoid Robotics Funding Tracker and Companies index, as of 1 September 2026. The numbers behind that gap are stark. Six companies have raised more than $500 million each. Together they hold $7.6 billion — roughly 65 percent of all disclosed capital in the sector. Every one of them is at pilot or prototype stage. Four companies have humanoids in general commercial availability. Together they have raised $1.03 billion, under 9 percent of the sector total. The largest of them raised $340 million. That is the finding worth sitting with. This is not the familiar observation that money and progress are imperfectly correlated. It is that at this moment, in this category, they are running on entirely separate tracks — and the reasons are engineering reasons, not financing ones. Capital raised versus humanoid platform stage, 26 companies with disclosed funding, September 2026. Source: The Robotic Life research.

sections.title: A Note on Method
sections.content:
The $11.7 billion total counts disclosed capital raised by humanoid robotics companies, including pre-IPO rounds for companies that have since listed. It excludes two things deliberately.

Internally funded corporate programs are counted separately. Tesla has disclosed more than $20 billion in dedicated capital expenditure and Xiaomi more than $10 billion in committed R&D across its EV and AI divisions. That is more than $30 billion, and it dwarfs everything else in the category — but it is a company deciding to spend its own money, not capital raised into a humanoid business. Folding it in would swamp the figure and make cross-company comparison meaningless.

Companies with undisclosed funding are excluded rather than estimated. Toyota Research Institute, Engineered Arts, Kawada, LG and several others publish no figure. Guessing would corrupt the total.

Stage refers to the humanoid platform only. Several companies here ship other robots commercially — Boston Dynamics’ Spot, Pudu’s service robots, JAKA’s cobots — while their humanoid sits at an earlier stage. The test for commercial is narrow and deliberately so: can a buyer place an order and receive a unit? Pilot means units are operating at sites the company does not own. Prototype means working hardware exists but has not left the building.

sections.title: Where the Money Is
sections.content:
Capital is concentrated but less extremely than the headlines suggest. The five largest positions account for roughly 59 percent of disclosed funding. The concentration splits into three lanes.

The American mega-round lane

Figure AI leads all private fundraising with $2.34 billion in cumulative capital at a $39 billion valuation, following a Series C exceeding $1 billion in September 2025. Apptronik holds $1.1 billion at a $5.5 billion valuation, with Mercedes-Benz and Google backing the Apollo program. Both are at pilot stage.

The European counterweight

NEURA Robotics holds $1.6 billion in total funding at a $7 billion valuation, following a Series C announced in June 2026 as up to $1.4 billion — a figure contingent on the company meeting stated performance milestones, and worth reading as a ceiling rather than a settled balance. The round was led by Tether, with NVIDIA, Amazon, Qualcomm, Bosch and Schaeffler participating. The 4NE-1 platform is at prototype stage.

The Asian lane, and the exception inside it

UBTECH raised more than $1 billion privately before listing in Hong Kong in December 2023, and has Walker S units operating at BYD, Foxconn, Zeekr and Audi FAW plants. XPeng Robotics raised more than $900 million at a valuation above $6.3 billion. Galbot holds $635 million at $3 billion. And then Unitree, which is the exception that makes the whole argument. Unitree reached commercial shipping and a public listing on roughly $155 million in pre-IPO private capital. Its G1 sells to anyone with a purchase order. It listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in August 2026. It raised about one fifteenth of what Figure has raised, and it is further along the commercial path than any Western company in the category.

sections.title: The Four That Ship
sections.content:
The commercially available column is short: Unitree, EngineAI, LimX Dynamics and Rainbow Robotics. Three are Chinese; Rainbow is a Samsung subsidiary listed in Korea. Their combined disclosed capital is $1.03 billion.

None of them raised a mega-round. EngineAI, the best-funded of the four, holds $340 million. LimX has $296 million and has filed for a Hong Kong listing. Rainbow holds $240 million.

What they share is not a technical breakthrough the others lack. It is a different product decision. These are units sold to buyers who want a capable platform — researchers, integrators, developers, factories willing to do their own integration work. They are not selling a general-purpose worker that arrives ready to replace a job. That is a narrower promise, and a shippable one.

The companies holding the large rounds are pursuing the broader promise. That is a defensible strategy with a longer horizon. But it is worth naming plainly: the reason $7.6 billion sits with companies that have not shipped is not that they are behind. It is that they are attempting something harder.

sections.title: The Readiness Ledger
sections.content:
Deployment status reorders the field completely, and pilot stage covers a very wide range.

Agility Robotics has the deepest operational record in the category. Digit has logged more than 65,000 operational hours per the company’s merger announcement, with enterprise customers including Schaeffler, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, GXO and Mercado Libre, more than $300 million in multi-year orders for the next-generation Digit V5 pending contractual milestones, and over 30 customers in its pipeline.

That figure is worth reading as an engineering metric rather than a marketing one. Cumulative hours across live customer sites is the closest thing this industry has to a reliability dataset: it is where mean time between failures, wear under real duty cycles and the actual frequency of human intervention get measured. Laboratory demonstrations do not generate that data. Only deployments do, and it compounds — the fleet with the most hours has the most failure modes already catalogued and engineered out.

Agility reached that record on approximately $180 million in pre-SPAC private capital, under 8 percent of what Figure has raised. It signed a definitive merger agreement with Churchill Capital Corp XI in June 2026 at a $2.5 billion pre-money equity value, targeting more than $620 million in gross proceeds and a listing as AGLT. Per the company’s description, it would be the first US-listed pure-play humanoid robotics firm with active commercial deployments.

It still sits at pilot stage on this chart, because you cannot order a Digit. That is not a criticism of Agility — it is a description of how enterprise robotics is sold, and it is why pilot stage spans everything from a single unit on trial to a fleet with 65,000 hours behind it.

sections.title: Three Filters Between a Funded Program and a Commercial One
sections.content:
Capital solves some problems and defers others. Three filters stand between a funded humanoid program and a deployed one. None is primarily financial.

Filter one: manipulation, not locomotion

Locomotion is substantially solved. The hard problem is contact-rich manipulation in unstructured environments, and the difficulty is data, not mechanics. Locomotion generalizes well from simulation. A walking gait can be modeled, domain-randomized and trained at enormous scale in simulation, then transferred to hardware with a manageable reality gap. Manipulation transfers poorly. Friction, compliance, deformable materials, occluded grasps and slip are precisely the phenomena physics engines approximate worst, so a large share of the training data has to come from the physical world — teleoperation, demonstration or deployed operation — at a cost per hour that does not fall the way GPU hours do. That is why capital flows toward data infrastructure and embodied-intelligence models rather than actuators. Money buys compute and funds data collection. It does not buy generalization on a schedule. For an operations leader the practical test is narrow and repeatable. Does performance hold when part presentation changes, when the bin is disordered, when lighting shifts, when a fixture is a quarter inch out of position? Every pilot is asking that question, which is why pilots take as long as they do — and why the companies selling capable platforms to technically sophisticated buyers can ship while the companies selling finished autonomy cannot.

Filter two: unit economics, measured at the cell rather than the robot

Acquisition price is the least interesting number in the deployment decision. The equation that governs is fully loaded cost per task-hour, and the robot’s price is one term in it. The others: integration and commissioning, fixturing and work cell modification, safety validation, charging or battery-swap infrastructure and the floor space it consumes, uptime, mean time to repair, spare parts and service response time, and — the term most often omitted from public analysis — the supervision ratio. A platform requiring one technician per two units is a fundamentally different business case from one requiring one per twenty, at identical hardware cost. A robot that works is not the same as a robot that pays. Cycle-time parity with a human operator is necessary and nowhere near sufficient; the machine has to hold that cycle time across a shift and across a quarter, without an engineer resident on the floor.

Filter three: the standards gap

This filter is the least visible in funding announcements and the most likely to govern the timing of scaled deployment. The governing industrial framework — ISO 10218-1:2025 and ISO 10218-2:2025, the latter having absorbed the collaborative-application requirements formerly held in ISO/TS 15066 — rests on an assumption that does not hold for this machine class: that a robot is statically stable. Remove power from a conventional industrial arm and it stops where it is. Remove power from a bipedal humanoid and it falls. Fall direction, distance and energy depend on velocity, payload and floor condition, and the existing framework does not address any of it. ISO/TC 299 has a project under development to close that gap. ISO/CD 25785-1 covers safety requirements for industrial mobile robots with actively controlled stability — legged, bipedal, quadrupedal or wheeled self-balancing platforms. It remains a committee draft rather than a published standard, which means integrators today assemble a compliance case from ISO 12100, ISO 10218 where it applies, IEC 61508 or IEC 62061 for system-level functional safety and ISO 13849-1 for safety-related control functions, rather than working from a single Type C standard written for the machine in front of them. Note who is writing it. The leadership of the U.S. delegation to ISO 25785-1 has included Kevin Reese of Agility Robotics as project leader and Federico Vicentini of Boston Dynamics, alongside Carole Franklin of the Association for Advancing Automation. The companies with the deepest operational records are also the companies drafting the rules that will govern deployment. That is not a coincidence, and it is not something a larger round can shortcut. Standards participation is earned with operational hours.

sections.title: Who Crosses Over Next
sections.content:
The forward question is which companies move from pilot into general availability. Five criteria separate them, all technical rather than financial, and all observable from outside.
  1. Repeat orders from the same site. A second purchase order from a facility that has already run a pilot is the highest-quality signal available, because that customer has seen the failure modes and bought anyway.
  2. Task breadth per deployment. A platform performing three distinct tasks at one site is closer to general-purpose economics than one performing a single task at ten sites. Breadth is what justifies the humanoid form factor over a purpose-built machine.
  3. A declining supervision ratio, disclosed. Almost nobody publishes it. The companies that begin to are the ones confident the trend is in their favor.
  4. Serviceability engineering. Field-replaceable actuators, hot-swappable batteries, documented mean time to repair, spare-parts logistics. Unglamorous, and it decides whether a fleet scales past a dozen units.
  5. Standards engagement. Active participation in ISO/TC 299 or A3 committee work signals a company planning for certified, permanent deployment rather than an indefinite sequence of pilots.
Watch the purchase orders, not the press releases.

sections.title: What to Watch Over the Next Twelve Months
sections.content: The AGLT close. Agility’s merger is expected to close in 2026 pending shareholder approval and regulatory clearance. The first US pure-play listing creates the category’s reference valuation and, more usefully, its first quarterly disclosure of humanoid unit economics. Unitree as the public comp. Post-listing trading gives the industry its first market-priced read on a lean, shipping-first humanoid business, against which every private valuation in the category will now be measured. LimX’s Hong Kong listing. A second shipping-first company reaching public markets would establish the pattern rather than the exception. The first order button in the West. No US or European company currently sells a humanoid to general buyers. Whichever does it first — and at what price, with what supervision requirement — sets the benchmark everyone else is measured against. ISO 25785-1 progression. When the dynamically-stable-robot standard advances toward publication, deployment planning changes for every integrator in the category. It is the least-covered item on this list and arguably the most consequential. Funding measures conviction. Deployment measures progress. The $11.7 billion already committed guarantees the race continues. The engineering decides who finishes it — and right now, the quadrant where funding and readiness meet is empty. The companies worth watching are the ones closing the distance, and that distance is measured in operational hours, supervision ratios and published standards, not in valuations. The dataset behind this analysis is maintained in The Robotic Life’s Humanoid Robotics Funding Tracker, updated monthly with primary-source verification, and the Companies index, which publishes deployment stage for every humanoid platform tracked. Lars Talbert is the founder of The Robotic Life, a data platform tracking the humanoid robotics economy: 38 robot platforms, the companies building them, and the capital funding them. He brings more than 30 years of market experience and more than 20 years in technology sales to the analysis. His work pairs verified specification data with funding intelligence at theroboticlife.com. title: From Robot Demo to Real Deployment
author: Randy Levine
description: Seven questions buyers should ask before investing in humanoid robots

sections.title: The readiness gap
sections.content:
A humanoid robot can lift a box in a demonstration, walk through a warehouse aisle or complete a carefully rehearsed sequence. Those moments are useful evidence of engineering progress. They are not, by themselves, proof that a robot can operate safely, reliably and economically throughout a commercial shift.

The central purchasing mistake is to treat a capability demonstration as if it were a deployment record. A sound evaluation starts with a narrower question: can this particular system perform our defined task, in our actual environment, with documented limits and a support model we can afford? The distinction matters as robotics adoption grows. The International Federation of Robotics reported approximately 542,000 new industrial robot installations worldwide in 2024. That is evidence of an established automation market, not evidence that every newly announced humanoid platform is commercially mature.

sections.title: 1. What task is the robot actually qualified to perform?
sections.content:
“General purpose” is an aspiration, not a usable procurement specification. Buyers should identify the exact workflow: the objects handled, their weights and dimensions, required precision, route complexity, interaction with people, and acceptable completion time.
Ask for a demonstration of the full task, including starting conditions and exceptions. If the robot transfers a tote, what happens when the tote is misaligned, a label is obscured or a pedestrian enters the aisle? A task-specific trial reveals far more than a highlight reel. A humanoid form factor may help in spaces designed for people, but it does not automatically outperform a mobile robot, conveyor, cobot or conventional lift truck.

sections.title: 2. How much human intervention does success require?
sections.content:
A video rarely shows every operator action. Clarify whether movements were autonomous, preprogrammed, remotely controlled or corrected by a human during execution. These modes are not inherently illegitimate; remote supervision can be a sensible deployment strategy. The problem arises when they are presented interchangeably.
Request an intervention log. Record the frequency, reason and duration of operator assistance, and distinguish routine monitoring from direct teleoperation. A robot that needs a remote operator for each exception may still deliver value, but the labor economics will differ from those of an autonomous system. Ask what happens during lost connectivity and how the machine reaches a safe state.

sections.title: 3. What reliability evidence exists outside a staged demonstration?
sections.content:
Availability should be measured over meaningful operating periods, not inferred from a successful short run. Buyers should ask for hours of operation, number of completed cycles, unplanned stops, recoveries, maintenance events and environmental conditions. They should also learn whether performance numbers come from a laboratory, a customer pilot or a routine production installation.
No single metric tells the whole story. “Uptime” may exclude scheduled maintenance, operator resets or time spent waiting for a task. Define the denominator before comparing vendors. If a supplier cannot share production data, an independently witnessed pilot with agreed measurement rules is a reasonable next step. Do not treat an announced pilot as proof of a scaled commercial rollout.

sections.title: 4. Has the safety case been assessed for this environment?
sections.content:
Robots introduce mechanical, electrical, control-system and human-interaction hazards. An industrial robot operating behind guarding presents a different risk profile from a mobile humanoid navigating shared workspaces. OSHA identifies hazards associated with industrial robot systems and points employers to hazard-recognition and safety resources. Applicable standards, local requirements and site-specific assessments should be evaluated with qualified safety professionals.
Before procurement, ask who owns the risk assessment, how emergency stops and protective measures work, what the robot does after a fault, and which tasks require restricted access or additional training. Review end effectors, pinch points, loads, batteries and charging equipment. Safety is not a marketing badge; it is an ongoing system-level responsibility involving the manufacturer, integrator and operator.

sections.title: 5. Is the product available to buy, or only available to discuss?
sections.content:
Robotics announcements often describe very different commercial stages. A public prototype, a limited research deployment, a reservation program and a product with contracted delivery dates are not equivalent. Buyers should request the exact model and configuration, the delivery commitment, the installation scope and the support geography.
A practical availability classification is: demonstrated prototype; controlled pilot; limited customer deployment; orderable product with defined terms; or repeatable commercial deployment. These are proposed reporting labels, not an industry standard. They make conversations clearer and prevent a preorder deposit from being mistaken for a machine ready to work next quarter.

sections.title: 6. What does the total cost of ownership include?
sections.content:
A purchase price is only the first line of a robotics business case. Depending on the application, costs may include end effectors, software licensing, integration, safety engineering, mapping, charging infrastructure, operator training, spare parts, field service, insurance and downtime.
Compare the full operating model with the current workflow and with less complex automation alternatives. For example, if the robot saves time on routine transfers but requires an attendant during exceptions, that supervision belongs in the cost model. Evaluate both an expected case and a downside case with slower throughput or higher intervention rates. Avoid extrapolating a vendor’s best-case demonstration into an annual return-on-investment promise.

sections.title: 7. Who is accountable after installation?
sections.content:
Procurement does not end at delivery. Establish who will provide updates, cybersecurity patches, replacement components, on-site repairs and incident support. Review warranty exclusions, service response times, software dependencies, data retention and the ability to export operational records. If the system uses cameras or remote access, clarify what information leaves the facility and who can access it.
Contractual acceptance criteria should be linked to the original task: measured throughput, intervention thresholds, safe operation, documentation and training. Buyers also need an exit plan if a pilot fails. A supplier with a compelling prototype but no realistic service network may be unsuitable for a time-critical operation.

sections.title: A practical pilot before a purchase order
sections.content:
A disciplined pilot can be straightforward. Define one workflow and its baseline performance. Set the trial period, site conditions and safety responsibilities in writing. Agree on success metrics before the vendor arrives. Record each intervention, fault and maintenance event. Include frontline operators in the evaluation, and compare the robot against both the existing process and feasible alternatives.
A useful scorecard includes task completion rate, throughput, intervention frequency, operational availability, safety observations, integration effort and fully loaded cost. Results should be reported with context rather than compressed into a single marketing percentage. When performance falls short, identify whether the issue is the robot, the environment or the task design before drawing broader conclusions.

sections.title: The real buying signal
sections.content: The next phase of robotics adoption will be shaped less by impressive individual demonstrations than by evidence of dependable work. Buyers do not need to dismiss humanoids or wait for perfection. They do need to ask precise questions, verify the answers and separate technical promise from commercial readiness. The best robot is not necessarily the one that looks most human. It is the system that can perform the required task safely, with measurable reliability, accountable support and economics that survive scrutiny. Randy Levine is a U.S.-based business and marketing professional involved in digital publishing and buyer-focused research. He is affiliated with WhichBot.net, a website covering humanoid robots, robotics buying information, pricing and product availability.

title: Melexis Collaboration
author: Julien Ghaye, PhD, Product Line Manager, Robotics at Melexis
description: How a Melexis Collaboration is Working to Develop the Touch-Enabled Robots of the Future
details:
The coming era of robotics is not simply about increasing capability, it is about fostering a new kind of integration between machines and their environments, as well as, perhaps more importantly, society as a whole. Robots are beginning to move beyond fenced-off production lines into homes, hospitals, warehouses, and fields — spaces that are inherently more dynamic, unstructured, and often shared with people.
This transition demands not only advances in artificial intelligence (AI) but also a reconsideration of the way robots perceive the world. In these environments, physical interaction is both unavoidable and often unpredictable, and this demands a true imitation of human senses, with touch being critical. Robots must not only decide what to do but understand how they are doing it: whether a grip is secure, whether contact has occurred, whether resistance has changed.
Realizing this vision requires more than isolated technological improvements. The convergence of feedback mechanisms, like tactile sensors, and smart and adaptive control systems, is an interdisciplinary challenge requiring extensive collaboration among electronic hardware, software, embedded systems, mechanical robotics, and mechatronics experts. This article explores how the work of Melexis and Brubotics, the Brussels Human Robotics Research Center of the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), offers one such example of how collaboration can help to unlock new frontiers in robotic interaction.

sections.title: The Drive for Intelligent Robotic Perception
sections.content: Modern robotic systems have achieved impressive precision and adaptability, particularly when equipped with high-accuracy vision systems and operating in repetitive applications. However, tactile perception, the ability to sense and interpret physical contact, remains comparatively limited. Many robots today are envisioned to utilize visual feedback and advanced force sensors, yet the practical integration of such sensors is often limited due to factors such as the prohibitive cost and the challenge of achieving the necessary precision. While effective in highly structured environments, this basic approach can fall short when robots are required to manipulate fragile or irregular objects, adjust grip dynamically, or interact safely with humans. Unlike the human sense of touch, which is a rich combination of pressure, direction, friction, and vibration, most robotic platforms operate with a comparatively narrow understanding of contact. For example, a lack of reliable shear force detection can limit a system’s ability to detect when grip is slipping. Without it, robots must rely on predefined grip strategies or overcompensate with force, increasing the risk of either dropping objects or damaging them. This also limits their ability to learn from interaction and adapt to changing conditions in real time, as the control systems’ modeling and understanding of gripping tasks is essentially limited. To compensate for the lack of multimodal touch feedback inherent in humans, robots require advanced tactile hardware that can deliver comprehensive 3D information, enabling more accurate perception and interaction with their environment. This parallelism of mirroring human operation also carries into the software side. Complex embedded software, such as edge AI, is crucial for robotic systems to interpret tactile data, especially in understanding and adapting to the complex interactions between robots and objects during gripping tasks that are not predefined. But AI development of complex physical interactions can be inherently time-consuming, especially if carried out in the real world. These challenges reflect a broader issue in robotics: the historical separation between sensing hardware and AI development. To advance meaningful robotic touch, hardware and software must not only improve but also evolve together, informed by shared use cases, common datasets, and coordinated design. It is this gap between sensor design and the practical applications in robotics that has driven the collaboration between Melexis and Brubotics.

sections.title: A Collaboration in Action: Melexis and Brubotics
sections.content: With the support of the Flemish Agency for Innovation and Entrepreneurship (VLAIO) project SKINAXIS, Brubotics, a consortium of eight Vrije Universiteit Brussels research groups, is undertaking the task of equipping robots with a real sense of touch using Melexis technology. The initiative is designed not only to address the technical problem of measuring contact forces accurately but also the equally complex challenge of using that data to enhance real-world robot performance. Central to the project’s hardware is Melexis’ latest innovation, designed from the ground up for the robotics market – Tactaxis®. Unlike conventional tactile sensors that typically detect only vertical (normal) pressure, the novel 3D magnetic tactile sensor can detect both normal and lateral (shear) forces with a high degree of accuracy and resolution. This is achieved through an elegant mechanical–magnetic design – a magnet embedded in a soft elastomer structure is displaced by external forces, and this displacement is measured by a Triaxis® 3D magnetic sensing IC below. With this configuration, every compact 6 x 6 x 4.4 mm3 tactile sensor transmits real-time vector data on contact force at up to 1000 samples per second, sensitive to 30 mN, with a normal force range of 5 N, and an overload resistance of 15 N, ensuring the smallest deviations are captured. Within the project, Brubotics’ role is to transform raw sensory data into practical robotic applications, showcasing innovative solutions for enhanced safety and precision in robotic interactions. This means developing AI algorithms, robotic control strategies and experimental environments required to allow robots to interpret sensor feedback, predict slippage, and regulate gripper force to maintain a secure grip of numerous objects without deformation. Rather than collecting training data from scratch — a slow and laborious process — Brubotics implemented a simulation-based training approach using NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim platform. By integrating physics-based models of the Tactaxis® sensor into virtual robotic systems, the Brubotics teams can expose their AI models to thousands of manipulation tasks in simulated environments. These digital twins included common variables such as object properties, surface friction, and dynamic interactions, allowing the models to learn rich contact behavior without the bottleneck of real-world data collection. The AI models are being continuously refined and validated through real-world tests with the support of Melexis, ensuring alignment between virtual and physical performance. A highly accurate mathematical model of the sensor is also being developed and undergoing experimental validation to characterize exact limitations. This rigorous process is allowing the teams to quantify the sensor’s performance per application use case, laying the groundwork for broader deployment. This work is inherently supported by the sensors’ small, light, and inexpensive design, compared to other alternatives, which makes them suitable for a wide range of applications.

sections.title: Potential Use Cases
sections.content:
While the research is ongoing and the AI model is being refined to further enhance system performance, Brubotics has successfully prototyped Melexis technology in a number of applications.
First is in rehabilitation and assistive robotics, where the team of researchers is exploring how robots equipped with Tactaxis® can be used to detect patient-initiated movement. Rather than acting as passive devices or rigid force applicators, the systems can instead more accurately infer movement intent and deliver proportionate, dynamic support — a crucial feature in devices like exoskeletons or therapeutic manipulators.
For generalized robotic manipulation, the collaboration between hardware and software entities shows how adaptive control based on accurate, 3D tactile data can improve the performance of grippers and robots. The project’s continued success highlights how engineers can design systems that detect changes in object stability and adapt gripping strategies – a crucial feature for humanoids, collaborative robots (Cobots), and autonomous mobile systems. This partnership uniquely combines public funding, academic research, industry know-how, and real-world testing, reflecting the complex process of robotic development to show how meaningful robotics applications can be accelerated from lab to deployment.

sections.title: Conclusion: Moving Towards a More Responsive Robotics Landscape
sections.content: While the Melexis-Brubotics collaboration focused on specific pilot applications, the implications extend much further. Tactile sensing of this kind, accurate, directional, compact, and cost-effective, has the potential to serve as a foundational capability for the next generation of robotic systems. For cobots, the ability to detect and interpret contact events, not just at the actuator, but at the surface, allows for safer, more flexible behavior. Rather than stopping entirely when encountering resistance, robots can assess whether a nudge is intentional, accidental, or a signal to adapt. Tactile sensing enhances the ability of robotic grippers to respond to variations in object weight, shape, or compliance — traits that are difficult to assess visually. It also supports the use of softer, more compliant materials, since control is no longer solely dependent on fixed grip force or predefined trajectories. Importantly, the rapid development of humanoid and service robots necessitates a true sense of touch. Here, this sense is vital for effective object handling and navigating environments that may be unpredictable, crowded, or specifically designed for human interaction. Tactile feedback enables these robots to adapt to minor contact, guide interaction through compliance, and behave in ways that are more intuitive for the people around them. For Melexis, this collaboration reflects a broader commitment to innovation. By engaging with university researchers, supporting student involvement, and contributing its engineering capabilities to shared challenges, the company aims to translate foundational technologies into systems with tangible societal impact. As robotics continues to expand beyond the factory and into everyday life, collaboration of all types will be keen to develop safe, reliable, and meaningful robotic interactions.
